newsitem.title: THAILAND: Ailing Thai economy seen recovering by end-1997.
newsitem.headline: Ailing Thai economy seen recovering by end-1997.

text.p: Thailand will weather its current economic problems and currency crisis, with its economy showing clear signs of an export-led recovery by late 1997, Socgen-Crosby Research Ltd said on Thursday.

Neil Saker, Socgen-Crosby's regional research head, said he also expected the Bank of Thailand to keep its two-tier baht exchange rate system for at least six to 12 months to ward off any further speculative attacks on the currency.

"The imposition of the dual currency market in May has proved highly successful. BoT has effectively squeezed the offshore market dry and is now the monopoly supplier of baht to the speculators as contracts mature," Saker told reporters.

He said the central bank's move to deny speculators access to offshore baht had restored its credibility, won international applause, and proved the effectiveness of regional repurchase pacts to protect Asian currencies against market attacks.

The central bank hit foreign baht speculators last month when it cut off their short-term baht supply by telling Thai banks not to lend baht to them or to make rates highly prohibitive. The move informally created a two-tier exchange rate system with one rate being quoted onshore and another offshore.
Saker said a better export performance in the second half of 1997 should help offset sustained weakness in the property and equity sectors.
He said projected 10 percent export growth this year should allow Thai gross domestic product (GDP) to expand by 4.5-5.0 percent this year, 5.5 percent in 1998 and about 7.0 percent a year later.
Official forecasts put GDP growth at 5.9 percent this year versus 6.4 percent in 1996.
Saker said, however, that Thai authorities needed to deal quickly with growing problems facing the country's troubled 91-company finance sector by allowing weak finance firms to fold.
"The authorities will have to bite the bullet and allow financial institutions to close. Essentially, the BoT must identify financial institutions which are able to survive and let the rest go under.
"If not done decisively ... probably in a few months, then there is a risk of a run on deposits affecting the entire system and capital flight," he told a media briefing.

Saker said Thailand's continued high overnight interbank rate of 10-12 percent made it impossible for domestic lending rates to ease, but any attempts to force interest rates down would increase its country credit risk and send wrong signals to investors.
Thai lending rates are among the highest in the region and have sparked a liquidity crunch that has hit the finance and property sectors hard.

The Bank of Thailand keeps interest rates high to attract capital inflows and fend off attacks on the baht. Some analysts have called for rates to come down significantly, to give the economy a much-needed boost.
Saker argued against a baht devaluation but said dramatic property price cuts were required to help speed up economic recovery.

He said Thailand's capital controls, by tightening baht supply in the offshore currency and equity markets, were not unique among Asian countries as Singapore, Taiwan and South Korea have adopted similar systems over the past 30 years.
Saker estimated that Thailand's foreign reserves may now have dropped to slightly over $30 billion after its market intervention to defend the baht in May from about $38 billion earlier.
He said, however, that the central bank was in a good position to replenish reserves because of its control of offshore baht supply.
Saker said the central bank made big foreign exchange gains from its effective intervention last month, leaving speculators with at least $1 billion in losses.
